newsitem.title: BELGIUM: European citizens eye free, safe, just zone.
newsitem.headline: European citizens eye free, safe, just zone.

text.p: A European area of freedom, security and justice may sound Utopian, but the bloc's 370 million citizens will judge next week's Amsterdam EU summit by how far their leaders move towards it.

At stake in the treaty review, aimed at preparing the bloc for the entry of up to a dozen, mostly east European countries, is a plan to do away with the passport controls between EU countries within five years.
At the same time the EU wants to strengthen its powers to crack down on the organised crime and breaches of asylum and immigration laws which leave citizens feeling vulnerable.
Under the accord taking shape, EU members will increase cooperation on controls at the bloc's outer borders and give the EU full powers over immigration and asylum policy.
They would also bolster cooperation between police and judicial forces against cross-border gangsters who trade in everything from drugs, to people, to arms.
The so-called Schengen Agreement, under which seven EU states operate a border-free zone, would become part and parcel of the EU, and all new members would have to sign up to it.

The Dutch, who as EU president, host the Amsterdam summit, hope that Britain, which as an island state wants to maintain full control over its borders, asylum and immigration policy and stay out of Schengen, will accept an "opt-out" from the scheme.

Denmark, too, has problems, dating back to the arrangements it negotiated when trying to make the 1992 Maastricht Treaty on European Union palatable to its people, who initially voted against the treaty in a referendum.
Women also have something to hope for in the new treaty, which would undertake to promote sexual equality.
The EU would also be given powers to act, unanimously, against discrimination on grounds of sex, racial and ethnic origin, religion and belief, disability, age, or sexual orientation.

As an oblique warning to prospective east European partners, EU members could find themselves losing their voting rights if they fail to honour fundamental freedoms such as liberty, democracy and respect for human rights and the rule of law.
